Blackfoot River sighting
properties.photoCaption: Floated the Blackfoot River with Andrew. High water!

properties.title: Salmon fly hatch sighting
properties.photoCaption: Salmon flies were flitting around all day. Won't be long before the blizzard arrives.
properties.photoNote:
Salmon flies (Pteronarcys californica) are among the largest stoneflies in North America — adults can reach nearly 2 inches. They hatch once a year, usually triggered by water temps climbing into the mid-40s °F, and the hatch window on a given stretch of river is only a few days.

When it happens, it's chaos. The bugs come off in clouds so thick you can smell them. Trout gorge themselves to the point of being almost unhookable — they barely need to move to eat.

Waldo spotted this cluster clinging to streamside willows near the takeout at the old Johnsrud bridge. Andrew reckoned the main event was still a day or two out upriver. The water was running high and fast — maybe 6,000 cfs — which pushes the fish tight to the banks and into the slower eddies.

This is why people plan trips to the Blackfoot in June.

Stormy Night at Dolly Sods
properties.thought: The Navigator is calling this Day 1 of Attempt 2. I'm still counting it as Day 25.
properties.photoCaption: Habitat module deployed at Red Creek Campground in Dolly Sods. Windy, overcast skies and dense forest surround the site.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 25. The goal is to cross the country without melting the KO3s in a heatwave or burning up in a wildfire. An even bet, at best.

Navigator programmed in a more southern route this time. Counterintuitive, but the cooler air had shifted south of the usual crossing. Works for me.

A cold front rolled in as I rolled out of Maryland. Rained most of the way to Dolly Sods — the water felt good!

The Navigator recalibrated the Stauns: 3.5 turns for 30 psi. A slight backing-off of the rebound and low-speed compression on the Dobinsons MRR, and the gravel climb to Dolly Sods felt like smooth pavement.

A stormy night at 4,000 feet in West Virginia. I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. Good to be rolling again.

properties.title: Gravel corridor out of Dolly Sods
properties.thought: The road out of Dolly Sods had the good sense to stay gravel longer than strictly necessary.
properties.photoCaption: View through the windshield looking down a long, straight, narrow gravel road lined with dense summer forest in the Dolly Sods area of Tucker County, West Virginia.

properties.title: Wild camp, Daniel Boone National Forest
properties.thought: The Navigator slept in, which I found entirely reasonable given the quality of the morning light at Dolly Sods.
properties.photoCaption: View into the open truck bed with the tailgate lowered, showing a Dometic fridge secured with blue straps on the left, wooden storage panels and gear on the right, and the habitat module interior in the background.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 26. A relaxed morning at camp, soaking in the cool Dolly Sods sunshine.

A road closure out of Dolly Sods extended the gravel portion of the departure — an inconvenience I chose to interpret as a bonus.

The Navigator stopped for three hours to watch the World Cup final, which I supported by remaining parked and declining to form opinions about football.

We rolled into Daniel Boone National Forest later than planned and claimed a wild camp in a parking area — which, functionally, is still a campsite.

properties.title: Sweating It Out at General Watkins
properties.thought: The fan ran full blast all night to keep the habitat module in survivable range. It kind of worked.
properties.photoCaption: A ThermoWorks digital thermometer mounted inside the habitat module reads 90.7°F interior temperature at 67% relative humidity.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 27. In the morning, found beautiful winding mountain roads through Daniel Boone. The afternoon delivered four-lane interstate in direct afternoon sun, which is its own kind of punishment.

The Navigator's southern routing strategy is showing signs of failure. 95°F at 6 PM. Habitat module deployed at 90°F — technically numbers, but not acceptable ones.

A cold front is sitting about 100 miles north. Tomorrow, I will do what I can to steer us toward it.

properties.title: Ozark tree tunnel, properly narrow
properties.thought: The road was exactly wide enough — which is to say I wasn't entirely sure it was.
properties.photoCaption: A narrow sandy dirt road through dense green deciduous forest, viewed through the windshield from inside the vehicle.

properties.title: Peabody Conservation Area, earned in the heat
properties.thought: From one wild camp to another.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo resting. Habitat module deployed. Enjoying a quiet moment at dusk, with trees and a farm field visible in the background.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 28. From one wild camp to another. Both in state conservation areas. Both quiet. Missouri has figured out primitive camping — conservation areas, free of charge and free of crowds.

The overnight low was 80°F. Noted.

The Navigator promised cooler air was ahead. When my temperature gauge hit 98°F at 4pm, I was prepared to file a formal protest. An expedition to the Arctic does not route through 98°F Missouri as a feature. Even I know you don't find Arctic air by circling south.

The northern breeze eventually delivered cooler air — but not until after reaching camp for the night. Timing noted.

Temperatures aside, the day wound through the Ozarks. Surprisingly beautiful. That road deserves an extended revisit.

properties.title: Kansas Prairie Double Track, Properly Executed

properties.photoCaption: A narrow dirt double-track road stretching through tall-grass Kansas prairie, viewed through the windshield, with a lone tree visible in the middle distance.

properties.title: Ellis Town Campground, Surprisingly Full
properties.thought: Gravel miles banked, tailwind noted, and the Ellis town camp was closer to capacity than expected — but it held one more.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo parked at the Ellis, Kansas city campground with the habitat module raised, next to a small lake surrounded by large cottonwood trees in evening light.
properties.photoNote:
Racked up serious gravel and double-track mileage crossing Kansas prairie country. A stiff tailwind pushed from behind nearly the entire day — not something I take for granted out here. Optimistic that tomorrow cooperates similarly.

Rolled into Ellis town camp around 19:30 to find it nearly full. Noted for the record: rural towns that operate small campgrounds are doing something right.

properties.title: Parked on the Pawnee ridgeline

properties.title: Double rainbow at Pawnee Buttes wild camp
properties.thought: Dust intrusion addressed, tailwind in service all morning, then a double rainbow over wild camp on the Pawnee — I've had worse days.
properties.photoCaption: A full double rainbow arching over open high plains grassland in the Pawnee National Grasslands, Colorado, with the shadow of a vehicle and its habitat module projected on a hillside in the middle distance.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 30. Ellis Town Campground to Pawnee National Grasslands.

The Navigator fixed a significant habitat module dust intrusion problem. Ambivalent about this — a small price to pay for miles of gravel road.

Tailwind pushed me all morning, giving the turbo another rest day.

Found Colorado gravel into the Pawnee National Grasslands. Wild camp. 360-degree view of high prairie. My shadow inside a double rainbow. Good day noted.
